name: ESP-DSP
baseline: The library's own non-optimized ANSI C implementations of the same DSP functions (the 'ANSI Xtensa' and 'ANSI Risc-V' columns), built with the same toolchain at -O2 and -Os
workload: CPU cycles per call for dot products (N=256), FIR/decimating FIR (1024 samples, 256 coefficients), radix-2/radix-4 float FFTs and 16-bit fixed-point FFTs (64 to 1024 points) and a biquad IIR (1024 samples): optimized assembly per chip versus the ANSI C version.
claimed_speedup: ESP32-S3 asm vs ANSI Xtensa at -O2: dsps_dotprod_f32 N=256 432 vs 1311 cycles (3.0x, derived from page data); dsps_dotprod_s16 N=256 307 vs 3635 (11.8x, derived); dsps_fft2r_sc16 1024 points 15,623 vs 221,955 (14.2x, derived); dsps_fir_f32 1024 samples/256 coeffs 443,671 vs 1,353,122 (3.0x, derived); dsps_fft2r_fc32 1024 points 97,847 vs 175,729 (1.8x, derived). ESP32-P4 dotprod_s16 208 vs 3385 ANSI Risc-V (16.3x, derived). Some rows show little or no gain: ESP32 dsps_fir_f32 1,078,691 vs 1,353,122 (1.25x, derived), ESP32-P4 dsps_fir_f32 1,606,563 vs 1,606,552 (parity), ESP32 dsps_fft2r_sc16 1024 points 226,154 vs 221,955 (no gain).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler optimization for speed (-O2 columns) and for size (-Os columns); compiler name and version not stated (ESP-IDF toolchain assumed)
hardware: ESP32 and ESP32-S3 (Xtensa) and ESP32-P4 (RISC-V); values are CPU cycle counts, clock speed not stated
stars_or_usage: 715 stars; official Espressif DSP component for ESP-IDF
tradeoffs: Assembly is per chip (ESP32, ESP32-S3, ESP32-P4); other targets fall back to ANSI C. Gains depend heavily on chip and function. Embedded targets only, not usable on desktop CPUs.
caveats: First-party table; compiler name and version and per-test clock are not stated. A benchmark source exists in the repo (test/prepare_csv_benchmarks.c, test_app/) but its contents were not opened. Several rows show no gain or a loss for some chips (see claimed_speedup). The README does not say how much of the assembly is hand-written versus generated. The single 'ANSI Xtensa' column does not say whether it was run on ESP32 or ESP32-S3.
found_via: GitHub: espressif/esp-nn README led to the sibling espressif/esp-dsp; opened github.com/espressif/esp-dsp and raw docs/en/esp-dsp-benchmarks.rst

name: ESP-NN
baseline: The library's own ANSI C reference kernels (selectable with the 'ANSI C' option under idf.py menuconfig NN_OPTIMIZATIONS) for TensorFlow Lite Micro int8 operators
workload: Ticks per kernel call for int8 convolution, depthwise convolution, pooling, fully connected, softmax, prelu, hard_swish, mean and elementwise add/mul at fixed small shapes, ANSI C versus optimized assembly.
hardware: ESP32-S3: 240 MHz, SPI QPI 80 MHz, 64 KB data cache; ESP32-P4: 360 MHz, SPI-RAM HEX 200 MHz, 128 KB L2 cache; ESP32-S31: 320 MHz, internal memory
stars_or_usage: 274 stars; kernel backend for TensorFlow Lite Micro on Espressif chips
tradeoffs: Assembly versions are selected only on ESP32-S3, ESP32-P4 and ESP32-S31; ESP32 and ESP32-C3 get generic C optimizations instead. Chip-specific, not portable to desktop CPUs.
caveats: First-party table of tick counts; compiler, flags and measurement method are not stated. Per-kernel test sources exist (tests/src/*_test.c, test_app/) but whether they produce these timings was not confirmed. The README says assembly versions exist but not that they are hand-written. Model-level timings (Person Detection, MobileNetV3, YOLO11n) compare with/without ESP-NN, not asm against C.
found_via: GitHub: espressif/esp-nn README (Kernelwise performance tables, ANSI C vs Optimized)

name: pqm4
baseline: The reference ('clean') C implementation of each post-quantum scheme, built with arm-none-eabi-gcc 11.3.1 at -O3 (and for BIKE the plain-C 'opt' implementation)
workload: Cycle counts for key generation, encapsulation/decapsulation and signing/verification of NIST post-quantum schemes (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, BIKE, others) on a Cortex-M4 at 24 MHz, reference C versus Cortex-M4 optimized (m4/m4f, 'typically in assembly') implementations.
claimed_speedup: ML-KEM-768 keygen/encaps/decaps: clean 988,722 / 1,138,225 / 1,387,984 cycles vs m4fspeed 642,096 / 658,754 / 707,827 (1.54x / 1.73x / 1.96x, derived from page data). ML-KEM-512 decaps 888,653 vs 428,167 (2.08x, derived). ML-DSA-44 signing 7,925,955 (clean) vs 3,943,121 (m4f) (2.0x, derived); ML-DSA-44 keygen 1,874,405 vs 1,426,025 (1.31x, derived). BIKE-L1 keygen 76,272,765 (opt C) vs 27,382,389 (m4f) (2.8x, derived). Averages of 10 to 1000 executions.
compiler_and_flags: arm-none-eabi-gcc (Arm GNU Toolchain 11.3.Rel1) 11.3.1 20220712; default build 'speed' = -O3 -g3 (mk/config.mk in mupq/mupq)
hardware: ARM Cortex-M4 at 24 MHz (README default board NUCLEO-L4R5ZI; stm32f4discovery also supported; the README does not say which board produced benchmarks.md)
stars_or_usage: 456 stars; reference benchmarking framework for PQC on Cortex-M4
tradeoffs: Cortex-M4 specific; m4 implementations trade stack/code size for speed (m4fstack variants use less stack). Each scheme directory has its own license.
caveats: Framework code is dual-licensed Apache-2.0/CC0 but every implementation subdirectory carries its own LICENSE/COPYING, so licensing is mixed. The 'm4' implementations are described as 'typically in assembly', so some speedup comes from C-level changes. The README carries a deprecation notice: no longer actively maintained, to be archived in or after January 2027. Board used for the published table is not stated.
found_via: GitHub: mupq/pqm4 README and benchmarks.md (recalled from PQC embedded benchmarking; opened on raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: FP-ASM (FP_ASM_LIB_DEV)
language: Assembly (NASM x86-64 AVX2) with a C API
baseline: Scalar C reference loops compiled with gcc 13 -O3 -march=native
workload: 100k-element f32 arrays, best of 200 runs: reduce sum, dot product, axpy, scale and a mat4 x vec3 batch transform; plus a 1M-star simulation (swarm_bench) FP-ASM versus plain C.
claimed_speedup: reduce sum (f32) 85.0 us scalar -O3 vs 9.9 us (8.6x); dot product (f32) 96.0 vs 18.9 us (5.1x); mat4 x vec3 batch 189 vs 122 us (1.5x); axpy 34.4 vs 34.2 us and scale 25.8 vs 25.7 us (parity). swarm_bench 1 thread on Emerald Rapids: total 7.01 vs 14.48 ms/frame (2.1x).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13, -O3 -march=native for the C reference; reproduce with make bench
hardware: Intel Core i7-4600M (Haswell, AVX2) for the kernel table; Intel Xeon Emerald Rapids (AVX-512), 4 vCPUs for swarm_bench
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2 only (NASM required); float reductions use several SIMD accumulators so results differ in rounding from a strict scalar sum. Memory-bound element-wise kernels gain nothing.
caveats: Wins come from reordering float reductions, which the compiler may not do at -O3 without -ffast-math, so the baseline is a strict-order scalar loop (outputs not bit-identical). Kernel table is one older laptop CPU; benchmark source files were not opened (README names make bench and benchmarks/). Young project (1 star).
found_via: WebSearch: github assembly language library faster than C compiler -O3 AVX2 NASM benchmark (result FP-ASM)

name: asmlib (abiiranathan)
language: Assembly (NASM x86-64 AVX2/BMI2; GNU as AArch64 NEON) with a C header and a portable C/wasm backend
baseline: glibc 2.44 memcpy/memset/memcmp/strlen/memchr/strstr/memmem, malloc/free, snprintf, sscanf and libm
workload: Nanoseconds per call from micro-benchmarks (bench/*.c) of asm_* routines against the glibc versions, best of 7 to 9 trials; function pointers are held volatile so the compiler cannot inline libc builtins.
claimed_speedup: memchr 1.1-1.2x from 128 B up; mid/large memcpy, memset, memcmp 0.95-1.2x (parity); strlen 0.5-0.8x and strstr 0.4-0.65x (glibc faster); memmem 'several times faster'. asm_snprintf 1.53-2.10x (mixed workload 159.32 vs 104.35 ns); asm_u64toa 80.81 vs 20.32 ns (3.98x); asm_sscanf 2.18-3.05x (sscanf %d 130.93 vs 44.78 ns). Arena allocator 4.36 vs 37.46 ns per op (8.59x) and malloc heap 4.79-8.08x; libm: cbrt 2.18x, sqrt 1.02x, most others 0.5-1.0x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2.1 and Clang 22.1.8 available on the test machine; benchmark build flags not stated (README example builds use cc -O2)
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U (Comet Lake) laptop, AVX2+BMI1+BMI2+ERMS+FMA, glibc 2.44, Linux 7.2
tradeoffs: Drop-in asm_* API rather than libc symbols; x86-64 needs AVX2/BMI2; AArch64 port uses NEON; math is freestanding C.
caveats: Author states the numbers are noisy laptop best-of-N results and that memory/string results are reported only qualitatively; glibc wins on strlen and strstr. The large arena and malloc-heap speedups come from a different allocation model (bump arena, thread-local cache), not from assembly alone. Single machine, benchmark flags unstated. Young repo with 0 stars.
found_via: WebSearch: github assembly language library faster than C compiler -O3 AVX2 NASM benchmark C API drop-in replacement (result asmlib)

name: oxsv
language: Assembly (NASM x86-64 AVX2) with a C build wrapper
baseline: xsv (Rust CSV toolkit); the microbenchmark compares the assembly SIMD scanners to a naive C loop
workload: 1 GB CSV (6.27M rows, 18 columns): count, headers, select, search, frequency, index, stats, sort, fmt; plus a 16 MB buffer byte-count/byte-find microbenchmark, assembly versus naive C.
claimed_speedup: count 0.17 s vs xsv 13.14 s (76x); select 0.82 vs 19.27 s (24x); frequency 1.14 vs 29.17 s (26x); sort 2.15 vs 47.58 s (22x); stats 12.97 vs 74.25 s (5.7x). SIMD microbenchmark: count_byte 8.9 vs 3.3 GB/s (2.7x), find_byte 11.3 vs 2.3 GB/s (5.0x), find_byte early exit 8 ns vs 88 ns (10.8x).
hardware: WSL2 on DDR4-3200; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Linux x86-64 only (AVX2 plus CPUID dispatch), mmap-based; join, sample, split, flatten and table are not implemented.
caveats: No CPU model, compiler or flags, no version of xsv, no run counts. The README itself notes search uses exact match by default whereas xsv uses regex, so that row is not like-for-like; oxsv memory-maps the file, which is an I/O strategy difference rather than a pure compute comparison. The 'naive C' baseline compiler flags are unstated, so the 2.7-10.8x SIMD rows may overstate against an auto-vectorizing -O3 build.

name: vxdiff
language: Assembly (AVX-512) with a C front end
workload: hyperfine runs of vxdiff against odiff on PNG pairs: one very large image, one very small image and one extreme-alpha image.
claimed_speedup: very large image 1.04 +/- 0.04 times faster than odiff; very small image 15.10 +/- 29.81 times faster; image with alpha 2.48 +/- 0.37 times faster.
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512; PNG only; the comparison routine is assembly (vxdiff.asm) while PNG decoding is done in C through libspng (main.c).
caveats: No license file was found (LICENSE returned 404 on the default branch), so the code is reference only. The README gives no CPU, compiler, image sizes or odiff version; the bench script is hyperfine -i -N on one pair per run. The small-image result has a standard deviation larger than the mean, and the large-image gain is within noise of 1x, which suggests PNG decoding rather than the compare loop dominates end-to-end time (not verified).

name: ademakov/bzero
language: Assembly (x86 SSE/AVX, GNU as) with C test harness
baseline: libc memset (bzero_0 in the harness) and the author's trivial and unrolled C versions compiled with gcc -O2
workload: Time to clear buffers of 0 to 2048+ bytes by size, comparing libc memset, trivial/unrolled C, SSE intrinsics, rep stosb, and hand-written SSE/AVX assembly versions.
claimed_speedup: Core i7-4850HQ: clearing 32 B takes 26 (bzero_6) / 23 (bzero_7) vs memset 86 (3.3x / 3.7x, derived); 64 B 26 vs 70 (2.7x, derived); 256 B 51 vs 82 (1.6x, derived); 1024 B 189 vs 149 and 2048 B 393 vs 241 (memset faster). Xeon E5520 (no AVX): 64 B 47 vs 71, 256 B 79 vs 127, 1024 B 265 vs 317, 2048 B 655 vs 664. The README update says newer AVX versions are faster than memset for any size, but those tables were not captured.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O2 for the C versions (README says -O3 and clang -O2 may replace the C code with memset); Makefile CFLAGS=-march=native
hardware: Intel Xeon E5520 @ 2.27 GHz (no AVX) and Intel Core i7-4850HQ @ 2.30 GHz (AVX)
tradeoffs: Strong only for small sizes and the SSE versions; the author concludes stock memset is better for large buffers when it can use AVX/AVX2. Public-domain dedication gives no patent grant.
caveats: Timing units and glibc version are not stated. Old CPUs; AVX-512 not tested. Per-size tables are noisy single runs. Author notes stock memset is 'sometimes unreasonably bad for small buffer sizes' on these CPUs, which modern glibc ERMS/AVX memset paths may have fixed. The newer AVX version results were not read.

name: rt_memcpy_cm
language: Assembly (ARM Cortex-M, GCC/IAR/Keil sources) with a C interface
baseline: RT-Thread's C rt_memcpy and the Keil C library memcpy
claimed_speedup: rt_memcpy 1261 ms; this assembly version 883 ms (1.43x, derived from page data); C library memcpy 906 ms (assembly 1.03x faster, derived).
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; distributed as an RT-Thread online package
tradeoffs: Cortex-M3/4/7 only; handles non-word-aligned addresses; uses LDMIA/STMIA multi-register transfers (up to 40 bytes per operation).
caveats: Single test with no MCU, clock or flags. The assembly beats the Keil C library memcpy by only about 3%; the headline gain is over RT-Thread's own C rt_memcpy. README is in Chinese; it attributes the code to the uC/OS vendor and says the speedup comes from the load/store-multiple instructions, not from assembly per se.

name: CvsAssemblyBenchmark
language: Assembly (GNU as, AVX2/FMA) with C harness
baseline: GCC 12.2.0 -O3 compiled C i-k-j dense matrix multiply (double precision)
workload: 200 x 200 x 200 double-precision matrix multiply repeated 1,000 times, five runs, outputs compared (max absolute difference 1.42e-14).
claimed_speedup: Mean internal timer C 3.043 s vs assembly 1.823 s per 1,000 multiplications (1.66x); about 2.63 vs 4.39 GFLOP/s.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -Wall -Wextra -fPIE -pie (GCC 12.2.0); assembly built with GNU as 2.40
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2/FMA only; single fixed matrix size; FMA changes rounding relative to separate multiply and add.
caveats: The C build has no -march, -mavx2 or -mfma flag, so GCC targets baseline x86-64 and cannot emit AVX2 or FMA; the baseline is handicapped, although the README says -O3 auto-vectorizes with AVX. The repo description says 'Assembly is ~150% faster' while the data show 1.66x. CPU model not given; toy project.

name: FastMemcpy
language: C (header-only FastMemcpy.h using SSE2/AVX intrinsics, no assembly)
baseline: System memcpy of gcc 4.9 and MSVC 2012
workload: Total milliseconds for many copies per size from 32 B to 8 MiB across aligned/unaligned source and destination combinations, plus a random-access run.
claimed_speedup: 32 B (16,777,216 copies, both aligned) memcpy_fast 81 ms vs memcpy 281 ms (3.5x, derived); 64 B 91 vs 364 ms (4.0x, derived); 512 B 124 vs 242 ms; 8 KiB 55 vs 70 ms; 8 MiB 287 vs 421 ms (1.5x, derived); random access 487 vs 1000 ms. Title claim: speed-up over 50% on average. At 1 MiB with both aligned memcpy_fast 181 ms is slower than memcpy 165 ms.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.9: gcc -O3 -msse2 FastMemcpy.c (AVX: -O3 -mavx FastMemcpy_Avx.c); msvc 2012: cl -arch:SSE2 -O2
tradeoffs: SSE2 or AVX only; jump table for small sizes, non-temporal stores and prefetch for huge sizes.
caveats: Implementation is SIMD intrinsics (85 _mm_ calls in FastMemcpy.h, no inline asm), so it is included for the memcpy baseline of this category, not as hand-written assembly. CPU model not stated and 2017-era libc/compilers (gcc 4.9, MSVC 2012) are far weaker than modern glibc ERMS/AVX memcpy; the gains likely do not hold today. Several rows show no gain.
found_via: WebFetch: github.com/skywind3000/FastMemcpy (recalled classic 'faster than memcpy' project)

name: chingrep
language: Assembly (hand-written ARM64 GNU assembler) and C (x86_64 AVX2 intrinsics)
workload: 22 search scenarios (literal, -i, -w, -c, -l, -m, include/exclude globs, frequency classes, stdin) over a 17,000+ file source workspace, minimum of 3 iterations.
claimed_speedup: Total arena time 1,870.9 ms (cg) vs 12,470.7 ms (rg), 6.7x faster overall; cg wins 21 of 22 scenarios; literal search 87.3 vs 641.0 ms (7.3x); exclude-dir 79.9 vs 670.3 ms (8.4x); include *.c 27.9 vs 37.9 ms (1.4x); piped stdin 3.6 vs 3.5 ms (rg wins).
hardware: Apple Silicon ARM64 (chip model not stated)
tradeoffs: Hand-written assembly only on ARM64 (src/asm/simd_arm64.s); the x86_64 path is AVX2 intrinsics in C and a portable C fallback exists.
caveats: Tagline claims up to 40x faster than ripgrep but the published table tops out at 8.4x. ripgrep version, flags and whether both tools searched the same file set (ripgrep honours ignore files and skips hidden/binary files by default) are not stated. Warm-cache single machine run. Only the ARM64 path is described as handcrafted assembly; source was not opened.
found_via: WebSearch: written in pure x86-64 assembly faster than ripgrep ... hyperfine benchmark github (result chingrep)

name: asmjson
language: Rust crate with hand-written x86-64 AVX-512BW assembly
baseline: sonic-rs (AVX2 lazy Value), simd-json and serde_json
workload: cargo bench on a single core over 10 MiB of synthetic JSON: string array, string object and mixed documents.
claimed_speedup: String array: asmjson/sax 10.78 GiB/s and asmjson/dom 10.93 GiB/s vs sonic-rs 6.92 GiB/s (1.56x and 1.58x, derived), serde_json 2.41, simd-json 1.91 GiB/s; string object: sax 8.29 vs sonic-rs 4.06 GiB/s (2.0x, derived); mixed: sax 1.17 GiB/s vs sonic-rs 478 MiB/s (2.5x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench (profile and RUSTFLAGS not stated)
hardware: Not stated for the main table (an example names a Ryzen 9 9955HX); needs Ice Lake or later Intel or Zen 4 or later AMD for AVX-512BW
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512BW (a portable SWAR fallback exists); Rust API only, no C ABI documented; README labels it experimental and not production ready.
caveats: Rust crate, so not directly usable from C++; baselines are Rust parsers, not a C/C++ compiler build. The simd-json row includes cloning the 10 MiB input on every iteration (README dagger footnote), so it is not like-for-like. Synthetic documents, CPU and flags unstated for the main table.
found_via: WebSearch: written in x86-64 assembly faster than simdjson ... github README benchmark (result asmjson)

name: cat-dog-asm-cnn
baseline: Equivalent NumPy-based CNN (and PyTorch, which it does not beat)
workload: Training/inference of a three-stage Conv2D+ReLU+MaxPool CNN with two dense layers on 25,000 128x128x3 cat/dog images (78% accuracy, same as the Python version).
claimed_speedup: 'Approximately 10x faster performance than an equivalent NumPy-based CNN'; README says it does not reach PyTorch speed (an earlier, more specialized project is said to have exceeded PyTorch by about 1.4x).
compiler_and_flags: NASM via build.sh; flags not listed
hardware: Not stated (container run with --cpus=4 --memory=4g; needs an AVX-512 CPU)
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512; whole network in assembly makes changes costly; slower than PyTorch.
caveats: No timings, workload split (training vs inference), NumPy code, hardware or flags are given, so the 10x figure is unverifiable. The NumPy baseline is not linked. Educational project.
